parts:
Try using a polychoric correlation matrix (which lavaan can generate from raw data)

fit.model1<-cfa(model1, data=DATAFRAMENAME, ordered=TRUE)

Per the tutorial pages, "...lavaan will automatically switch to the WLSMV estimator: it will use diagonally weighted least squares (DWLS) to estimate the model parameters, but it will use the full weight matrix to compute robust standard errors, and a mean- and variance-adjusted test stastistic."

parts: How to obtain WLS.V and NACOV?

From lavCor() when you request to output a lavaan object.  This thread should be helpful:  https://groups.google.com/d/msg/lavaan/KZFGMlCuCDo/ayI3MNDSAAAJ

But it is not at all clear from your posts why you need this.  You have the raw data, right?  To use DWLS, you need the raw data and to tell lavaan the variables are ordered.  To use MLM or MLR, you also need raw data, but do not tell lavaan to treat the variables as ordered.

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: CFA ordinal data how can I run it in Lavaan
parts: when I run the CFA in MLM or MLR the fit indices are regular.

I don't know what you mean by that.  There should be 2 columns in the summary() output.  The rightmost column of fit measures will be labeled "Robust", which is the column to pay attention to.  But you can only obtain those robust measures when you pass it raw data= to be treated as continuous, not a sample.cov=.
When I try to run it in WLSMV Lavaan warning Some estimated ov variances are negative appears.

Yes, Heywood cases happen sometimes, and they become more common (whether your model is correct or not) when your sample size is small relative to how many parameters you estimate.  You only have about 606/143 ~ 4 people per parameter, which is lower than the smallest recommended ratio I have ever seen in the SEM literature (5 people per parameter).

Because you have 6 thresholds per indicator (i.e., 7 categories), the best advice is to treat these data as continuous and use MLM (complete data) or MLR (incomplete data + FIML).

http://psychmodels.ucdavis.edu/uploads/8/6/3/9/86398102/rhemtullabrosseauliardsavalei_pm.pdf

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

El lunes, 26 de octubre de 2020 a las 6:41:51 UTC-4, Terrence Jorgensen escribió:
when I run the CFA in MLM or MLR the fit indices are regular.

I don't know what you mean by that.  There should be 2 columns in the summary() output.  The rightmost column of fit measures will be labeled "Robust", which is the column to pay attention to.  But you can only obtain those robust measures when you pass it raw data= to be treated as continuous, not a sample.cov=.
 
When I try to run it in WLSMV Lavaan warning Some estimated ov variances are negative appears. 

Yes, Heywood cases happen sometimes, and they become more common (whether your model is correct or not) when your sample size is small relative to how many parameters you estimate.  You only have about 606/143 ~ 4 people per parameter, which is lower than the smallest recommended ratio I have ever seen in the SEM literature (5 people per parameter).

Because you have 6 thresholds per indicator (i.e., 7 categories), the best advice is to treat these data as continuous and use MLM (complete data) or MLR (incomplete data + FIML).

http://psychmodels.ucdavis.edu/uploads/8/6/3/9/86398102/rhemtullabrosseauliardsavalei_pm.pdf

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: CFA ordinal data how can I run it in Lavaan
parts: I'm not sure in what part of the syntax I need to write lavInspect(fit, "cov") or if this warning is related to other thing.

lavaan is telling you to use the lavInspect() function to see why your latent covariance matrix is NPD:

(Psi <- lavInspect(fit.model1, "cov.lv"))

If the determinant is negative, there is linear dependency among the factors:

det(Psi)

As Pat pointed out, the linear dependency is probably related to the nearly perfect correlation between 2 factors.  EF and INT are correlated so highly, knowing the correlation of another factor with EF already tells you what the correlation of that factor with INT must be.  Thus, Psi contains redundant information (linear dependency).  If you were using this set of 5 factors to predict an outcome, then it is usually referred to as multicollinearity.  I would follow Pat's advice to reconsider the meaning of the indicators and consider whether they all measure the same factor. Of course, your model doesn't fit well, so perhaps the correlation is inflated for other reasons.  Instead of looking at modification indices, try looking at the correlation residuals to see which specific observed correlations your model fails to reproduce closely.  

lavResiduals(fit.model1, type = "cor")

Patterns of high discrepancies (e.g., > .1 in absolute value) in that matrix could help you think of alternative models, rather than asking modification indices to do that for you (which prior research has shown is an endeavor doomed to fail unless your model is almost perfect already).

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen
